questions.scenario: A start‑up company has no formal quality management system. Production decisions are made on a case‑by‑case basis by the production manager. A batch fails because of inconsistent raw material checks.
questions.question: What is the fundamental missing element according to PIC/S?
options: A. A system to track employee vacation days
B. A wide‑ranging Quality Management system covering all matters that influence product quality
C. An environmental monitoring programme
D. A contract with a third‑party logistics provider
questions.explanation: Clause 1.1 defines Quality Management as a wide‑ranging concept covering all matters that influence product quality. The company lacks an overall system, leading to inconsistent decisions.

questions.scenario: A manufacturer applies GMP strictly during commercial production but does not document technology transfer activities or control investigational product batches. An impurity issue traced to the transfer phase is missed.
questions.question: What does Clause 1.2 state about the scope of GMP?
options: A. GMP only applies after marketing authorisation is granted
B. GMP applies only to sterile product manufacturing
C. GMP applies to lifecycle stages from investigational products through technology transfer to commercial manufacturing and discontinuation
D. GMP is optional for clinical trial materials
questions.explanation: Clause 1.2: 'GMP applies to the lifecycle stages from the manufacture of investigational medicinal products, technology transfer, commercial manufacturing through to product discontinuation.'

questions.scenario: A small generic company copies the Pharmaceutical Quality System (PQS) of a large multinational without adjusting it. The system is bureaucratic and inefficient, causing delays.
questions.question: What principle of PQS design (Clause 1.3) is being ignored?
options: A. All PQS must be identical across companies
B. The size and complexity of the company's activities should be considered when developing or modifying a PQS
C. The PQS must be approved by the national regulator
D. Only large companies need a documented PQS
questions.explanation: Clause 1.3: 'The size and complexity of the company's activities should be taken into consideration when developing a new Pharmaceutical Quality System or modifying an existing one.'

questions.scenario: Senior management has not defined responsibilities for outsourced activities. No system monitors process performance. A contract sterilisation failure goes undetected, leading to a recall.
questions.question: Which specific PQS objectives from Clause 1.4 were violated?
options: A. Product realisation and continuous improvement
B. Processes to assure management of outsourced activities and a state of control through monitoring
C. Only batch release requirements
D. Only self‑inspection
questions.explanation: Clause 1.4(vii) requires processes for outsourced activities; (viii) requires a state of control via monitoring. Both were absent.

questions.scenario: The CEO delegates the entire PQS to the QA manager and never reviews quality data. A major deviation is hidden by production, and the CEO is unaware.
questions.question: What does Clause 1.5 require of senior management?
options: A. Senior management has no role in quality
B. Senior management must approve every deviation
C. Senior management has ultimate responsibility to ensure an effective PQS is in place and adequately resourced
D. Senior management only needs to review budgets
questions.explanation: Clause 1.5: 'Senior management has the ultimate responsibility to ensure an effective Pharmaceutical Quality System is in place, adequately resourced and that roles, responsibilities, and authorities are defined, communicated and implemented throughout the organisation.'

questions.scenario: The company has never conducted a management review of its PQS. A recurring contamination problem is never escalated, and corrective actions are not implemented.
questions.question: What does Clause 1.6 mandate?
options: A. A one‑time internal audit
B. Periodic management review of the PQS operation to identify opportunities for continual improvement
C. Only annual product quality reviews
D. No formal review is required if no complaints are received
questions.explanation: Clause 1.6: 'There should be periodic management review… of the operation of the Pharmaceutical Quality System to identify opportunities for continual improvement of products, processes and the system itself.'

questions.scenario: A manufacturer has no Quality Manual or equivalent documented description of its quality system. Employees are unaware of management responsibilities, leading to role confusion.
questions.question: What does Clause 1.7 require?
options: A. Only batch records need to be documented
B. A Quality Manual or equivalent documentation describing the quality management system and management responsibilities
C. A verbal description of the system is sufficient for small companies
D. Only the regulatory filing is needed
questions.explanation: Clause 1.7: 'A Quality Manual or equivalent documentation should be established and should contain a description of the quality management system including management responsibilities.'

questions.scenario: A significant deviation (temperature excursion) occurs during granulation. The operator notes it in the margin but does not investigate. Three months later, the same deviation recurs and causes a failure.
questions.question: Which basic GMP requirement from Clause 1.8 was violated?
options: A. Validation of critical steps
B. Any significant deviation must be fully recorded, investigated to determine root cause, and CAPA implemented
C. Procedures must be written in clear language
D. Distribution must minimise risk to quality
questions.explanation: Clause 1.8(vii): 'Any significant deviations are fully recorded, investigated with the objective of determining the root cause and appropriate corrective and preventive action implemented.'

questions.scenario: A batch of tablets is released for sale before an Authorised Person certifies it. A later inspection reveals that the batch failed a critical impurity test.
questions.question: What does Clause 1.9 require regarding batch release?
options: A. Production can release if the batch passes in‑house tests
B. No batch may be released prior to certification by an Authorised Person that it complies with the MA and regulations
C. Only sterile products require Authorised Person certification
D. The QA manager can release batches without certification if QC results are satisfactory
questions.explanation: Clause 1.9(vii): 'No batch of product is released for sale or supply prior to certification by an Authorised Person that it is in accordance with the requirements of the relevant authorisations.'

questions.scenario: A company has not performed a product quality review for three years. A stability trend showing increasing impurities is missed, and several batches are later recalled.
questions.question: What does Clause 1.10 require?
options: A. Reviews are optional for low‑volume products
B. Regular periodic (usually annual) quality reviews, including review of stability trends, deviations, and changes
C. Only new products need a review
D. The Marketing Authorisation holder is solely responsible for reviews
questions.explanation: Clause 1.10: 'Regular periodic or rolling quality reviews… should normally be conducted and documented annually, taking into account previous reviews' and includes review of stability results.

questions.scenario: The product quality review identified a need for corrective action on a tablet press, but no action was taken. The same press caused another batch failure.
questions.question: What does Clause 1.11 require?
options: A. The manufacturer must evaluate review results and decide whether corrective/preventive action or revalidation is needed
B. No action is required if the product still passes tests
C. Only the MAH must act on review findings
D. Actions are optional if documented
questions.explanation: Clause 1.11: 'The manufacturer… should evaluate the results of the review and an assessment made as to whether corrective and preventive action or any revalidation should be undertaken.'

questions.scenario: A company makes risk decisions based on gut feeling without a documented process. A high‑risk change is implemented without assessment, leading to a contamination event.
questions.question: What is Quality Risk Management as defined in Clause 1.12?
options: A. A systematic process for assessment, control, communication and review of risks to quality
B. An informal meeting among department heads
C. A tool used only for sterile product manufacturing
D. A one‑time assessment at product launch
questions.explanation: Clause 1.12: 'Quality Risk Management is a systematic process for the assessment, control, communication and review of risks to the quality of the medicinal product.'

questions.scenario: A company documents a full risk assessment with extensive FMEA for a low‑risk change (changing the colour of a label). The effort consumes weeks of work.
questions.question: What principle of Quality Risk Management (Clause 1.13) is being ignored?
options: A. Risk evaluation must be based on scientific knowledge only
B. The level of effort, formality and documentation must be commensurate with the level of risk
C. Risk management must always be retrospective
D. Patient protection is the only factor
questions.explanation: Clause 1.13(ii): 'The level of effort, formality and documentation of the Quality Risk Management process is commensurate with the level of risk.'

questions.scenario: A small manufacturer has only one qualified person who is responsible for production, QC, and batch release. The person is overworked, and a critical batch is released without proper QC review.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.1 require to prevent such situations?
options: A. One person can handle all roles if properly trained
B. An adequate number of personnel with necessary qualifications; responsibilities on any one individual should not be so extensive as to present a risk to quality
C. Only production staff are needed; QC can be outsourced
D. No limit on responsibilities as long as the person is competent
questions.explanation: Clause 2.1: 'The manufacturer should have an adequate number of personnel with the necessary qualifications and practical experience… The responsibilities placed on any one individual should not be so extensive as to present any risk to quality.'

questions.scenario: The company has no organisation chart. During an inspection, the auditor cannot identify the head of Production or the Authorised Person, and there is confusion about reporting lines.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.2 require?
options: A. A verbal description of roles is sufficient
B. An organisation chart showing relationships between heads of Production, QC, and the position of Authorised Person(s) in the managerial hierarchy
C. Only a list of employee names is needed
D. A chart is required only for sterile product manufacturing
questions.explanation: Clause 2.2: 'The manufacturer must have an organisation chart in which the relationships between the heads of Production, Quality Control… and the position of the Authorised Person(s) are clearly shown in the managerial hierarchy.'

questions.scenario: A QC technician performs analytical work but has no written job description. His duties overlap with those of a production operator, leading to unauthorised sampling.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.3 require for responsible positions?
options: A. Verbal instructions are sufficient for small teams
B. People should have specific duties recorded in written job descriptions and adequate authority
C. Only senior management needs job descriptions
D. Job descriptions are optional if roles are understood
questions.explanation: Clause 2.3: 'People in responsible positions should have specific duties recorded in written job descriptions and adequate authority to carry out their responsibilities.'

questions.scenario: Senior management has not established a quality policy. Quality objectives are not communicated, and employees do not know the company’s quality direction.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.4 require of senior management?
options: A. No policy is needed if the company is small
B. Senior management should establish a quality policy describing overall intentions and direction related to quality
C. Only the QA manager can set the quality policy
D. The policy can be verbal and changed at any time
questions.explanation: Clause 2.4: 'Senior management should establish a quality policy that describes the overall intentions and direction of the company related to quality…'

questions.scenario: The head of Production also acts as head of Quality Control. He approves his own batch records and releases product without independent QC review. A batch with a deviation is released.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.5 require regarding these roles?
options: A. One person can hold both positions if qualified
B. The heads of Production and Quality Control must be independent from each other
C. Independence is only required for sterile products
D. A single head of Quality can oversee both functions
questions.explanation: Clause 2.5: 'The heads of Production and Quality Control must be independent from each other.'

questions.scenario: An Authorised Person certifies a batch without checking that it complies with the Marketing Authorisation (a test for a specific impurity was omitted). The batch is released and later recalled.
questions.question: What is a key duty of the Authorised Person per Clause 2.6?
options: A. Ensure each batch has been manufactured and checked in compliance with the Marketing Authorisation
B. Only sign the certificate after production approval
C. Delegate all responsibilities to the head of QC
D. Only check the batch record for completeness
questions.explanation: Clause 2.6(a): 'An Authorised Person must ensure that each batch of medicinal products has been manufactured and checked in compliance with the laws… and in accordance with the requirements of the Marketing Authorisation.'

questions.scenario: Production records are not evaluated before batch release, and staff in the production department have not received any training on GMP. A deviation is missed, and the batch fails.
questions.question: Which responsibilities of the head of Production (Clause 2.7) were neglected?
options: A. Ensure products are produced and stored according to documentation
B. Ensure production records are evaluated and signed by an authorised person, and ensure training of department personnel
C. Only supervise operators during processing
D. Approve raw materials and packaging materials
questions.explanation: Clause 2.7(iii) and (vi) require the head of Production to ensure production records are evaluated and signed, and to ensure training of department personnel.

questions.scenario: The QC head approves specifications but does not ensure that all necessary testing is carried out. A batch is released with incomplete testing, and a contaminant is missed.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.8 require of the head of QC?
options: A. Only manage laboratory staff schedules
B. Approve or reject materials and products, and ensure all necessary testing is carried out and records evaluated
C. Only sign certificates of analysis
D. Delegate all testing to external labs without oversight
questions.explanation: Clause 2.8(i) and (ii): the head of QC has responsibilities to approve/reject materials and products, and ensure all necessary testing is carried out.

questions.scenario: No one is responsible for monitoring the manufacturing environment. During an inspection, high particle counts are found, and contamination is traced to a lack of environmental control.
questions.question: According to Clause 2.9, which shared responsibility was neglected?
options: A. The monitoring and control of the manufacturing environment
B. Only cleaning validation
C. Only documentation of batch records
D. Only supplier approval
questions.explanation: Clause 2.9(ii): Shared responsibilities include 'the monitoring and control of the manufacturing environment.'

questions.scenario: A maintenance mechanic enters a production area to repair a mixer. He has never received GMP training and leaves a wrench inside the mixer, contaminating the next batch.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.10 require regarding training?
options: A. Only operators need GMP training
B. Training for all personnel whose duties take them into production areas, including maintenance and cleaning personnel
C. Training is optional for maintenance staff if they are supervised
D. Only new recruits need initial training
questions.explanation: Clause 2.10: 'The manufacturer should provide training for all the personnel whose duties take them into production and storage areas or into control laboratories (including the technical, maintenance and cleaning personnel).'

questions.scenario: Initial training is given to new employees, but no continuing training is provided, and its effectiveness is never assessed. Old mistakes recur, and a repeat deviation occurs.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.11 require beyond initial training?
options: A. One‑time training is sufficient for GMP compliance
B. Continuing training should be given, and its practical effectiveness should be periodically assessed
C. No records of training are required
D. Only supervisors need ongoing training
questions.explanation: Clause 2.11: 'Continuing training should also be given, and its practical effectiveness should be periodically assessed.'

questions.scenario: Personnel working with highly active cytotoxics receive only basic GMP training, no specific training on containment or decontamination. A spill occurs, exposing operators.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.12 require for such personnel?
options: A. Basic GMP training is sufficient for all areas
B. Personnel working in contamination hazard areas (e.g., highly active, toxic, infectious materials) should be given specific training
C. Only external experts can provide such training
D. No special training is needed if PPE is provided
questions.explanation: Clause 2.12: 'Personnel working in areas where contamination is a hazard, e.g. clean areas or areas where highly active, toxic, infectious or sensitising materials are handled, should be given specific training.'

questions.scenario: A visitor is taken into a production area without any advance information or supervision. They touch an exposed product surface, causing contamination.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.13 require for visitors?
options: A. Visitors can enter freely if they sign a log
B. Visitors should preferably not be taken into production areas; if unavoidable, they should be given information in advance and closely supervised
C. Only written authorisation from the CEO is needed
D. No restrictions apply to visitors
questions.explanation: Clause 2.13: 'Visitors or untrained personnel should, preferably, not be taken into the production and quality control areas. If this is unavoidable, they should be given information in advance… They should be closely supervised.'

questions.scenario: Training sessions focus only on equipment operation and never discuss the Pharmaceutical Quality System or how to improve quality. Employees are unaware of quality objectives.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.14 require in training?
options: A. Only technical training is needed
B. The PQS and all measures capable of improving its understanding and implementation should be fully discussed during training sessions
C. Training is only required for new hires
D. Quality topics can be covered in separate meetings
questions.explanation: Clause 2.14: 'The Pharmaceutical Quality System and all the measures capable of improving its understanding and implementation should be fully discussed during the training sessions.'

questions.scenario: No written hygiene programme exists. Operators wear street clothes in production areas, and handwashing is not enforced. A batch is contaminated by operator shedding.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.15 require?
options: A. Hygiene is left to individual discretion
B. Detailed hygiene programmes should be established, including procedures relating to health, hygiene practices and clothing of personnel
C. Only handwashing is required
D. Hygiene is only important for sterile product manufacturing
questions.explanation: Clause 2.15: 'Detailed hygiene programmes should be established and adapted to the different needs within the factory. They should include procedures relating to the health, hygiene practices and clothing of personnel.'

questions.scenario: A new operator is hired and placed in a granulation area without any medical examination. Later, it is discovered they have a chronic skin condition that could shed microbes.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.16 require?
options: A. Medical examination is optional for production staff
B. All personnel should receive medical examination upon recruitment
C. Only personnel handling sterile products need medical checks
D. Examination can be performed after one year of employment
questions.explanation: Clause 2.16: 'All personnel should receive medical examination upon recruitment.'

questions.scenario: An operator with an open wound on their hand is allowed to handle unpackaged tablets. The wound is not covered, and the batch later fails microbial testing.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.17 require?
options: A. No restriction as long as the wound is cleaned
B. Steps should be taken to ensure no person affected by an infectious disease or having open lesions is engaged in manufacture
C. Only if the wound is bleeding
D. A simple adhesive bandage is sufficient
questions.explanation: Clause 2.17: 'Steps should be taken to ensure as far as is practicable that no person affected by an infectious disease or having open lesions on the exposed surface of the body is engaged in the manufacture of medicinal products.'

questions.scenario: An operator enters a granulation area wearing only a lab coat and no hairnet or beard cover. Hair falls into the powder blend.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.18 require?
options: A. No protective clothing needed for oral solid dosage forms
B. Every person entering manufacturing areas should wear protective garments appropriate to the operations
C. Only supervisors need to wear full gowning
D. A simple apron is enough for all areas
questions.explanation: Clause 2.18: 'Every person entering the manufacturing areas should wear protective garments appropriate to the operations to be carried out.'

questions.scenario: An operator eats a sandwich at a workbench in the production area during a break. Crumbs fall into an open container of excipient.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.19 say about such practices?
options: A. Allowed if no product is present at that moment
B. Eating, drinking, chewing or smoking in the production and storage areas should be prohibited
C. Only smoking is prohibited
D. Allowed if the operator washes hands afterwards
questions.explanation: Clause 2.19: 'Eating, drinking, chewing or smoking… in the production and storage areas should be prohibited.'

questions.scenario: An operator uses bare hands to pick up tablets from a tray and place them into a container. The operator has not washed hands after using the restroom.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.20 require?
options: A. Bare hand contact is allowed if gloves are not available
B. Direct contact should be avoided between operator's hands and exposed product or equipment that contacts product
C. Gloves are only required for sterile products
D. Handwashing is sufficient to allow direct contact
questions.explanation: Clause 2.20: 'Direct contact should be avoided between the operator's hands and the exposed product as well as with any part of the equipment that comes into contact with the products.'

questions.scenario: The production area has no hand‑washing facilities. Operators must walk to the break room to wash hands, and often skip it due to distance.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.21 require?
options: A. No handwashing is necessary if gloves are worn
B. Personnel should be instructed to use hand‑washing facilities (implying that such facilities must exist and be accessible)
C. Hand sanitizer is an acceptable alternative to washing
D. Only after using the toilet is handwashing required
questions.explanation: Clause 2.21: 'Personnel should be instructed to use the hand‑washing facilities.' This implies the facilities must be provided.

questions.scenario: The company manufactures sterile products but applies only the general hygiene rules of Chapter 2, ignoring the more stringent requirements of Annex 1. A sterility failure occurs.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.22 state about special groups of products?
options: A. General rules are sufficient for all products
B. Any specific requirements for special groups (e.g., sterile preparations) are covered in the annexes
C. Annexes are optional guidance
D. Only the manufacturer can decide the requirements
questions.explanation: Clause 2.22: 'Any specific requirements for the manufacture of special groups of products, for example sterile preparations, are covered in the annexes.'

questions.scenario: The company hires a consultant with no GMP experience to advise on a critical validation project. No records of qualifications are kept. The consultant gives incorrect advice.
questions.question: What does Clause 2.23 require for consultants?
options: A. Anyone can be a consultant if they have industry experience
B. Consultants should have adequate education, training, and experience; records of name, address, qualifications, and service type should be maintained
C. No records of consultants are needed if they work through an agency
D. Only external auditors can act as consultants
questions.explanation: Clause 2.23: 'Consultants should have adequate education, training, and experience… Records should be maintained stating the name, address, qualifications, and type of service provided.'

questions.scenario: A pharmaceutical plant is built next to a chemical factory that emits corrosive fumes. No additional protective measures are taken. Over time, metal surfaces corrode, and particles contaminate products.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.1 require regarding premises location?
options: A. The environment does not matter if the building is sealed
B. Premises should be situated in an environment which, together with protective measures, presents minimal risk of causing contamination
C. Only the internal design of the plant matters
D. Any location is acceptable as long as final product is tested
questions.explanation: Clause 3.1: 'Premises should be situated in an environment which, when considered together with measures to protect the manufacture, presents minimal risk of causing contamination of materials or products.'

questions.scenario: A wall in the production area has a hole that is never repaired. Dust accumulates and falls into open containers. The cleaning procedure does not mention wall repairs.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.2 require?
options: A. Only cleaning is required, not maintenance
B. Premises should be carefully maintained; repair and maintenance must not hazard product quality; cleaning and disinfection according to written procedures
C. Maintenance can be performed during production hours
D. Holes are acceptable if they are small
questions.explanation: Clause 3.2: 'Premises should be carefully maintained, ensuring that repair and maintenance operations do not present any hazard to the quality of products. They should be cleaned and, where applicable, disinfected according to detailed written procedures.'

questions.scenario: The production area has poor lighting, making it impossible to see whether powder is correctly dispensed. Temperature is not controlled, causing a heat‑sensitive API to degrade.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.3 require?
options: A. Only lighting is important
B. Lighting, temperature, humidity and ventilation should be appropriate and not adversely affect product or equipment function
C. Only temperature control matters
D. No requirements for environmental conditions
questions.explanation: Clause 3.3: 'Lighting, temperature, humidity and ventilation should be appropriate and such that they do not adversely affect, directly or indirectly, either the medicinal products during their manufacture and storage, or the accurate functioning of equipment.'

questions.scenario: The warehouse has gaps under doors; insects and rodents are frequently seen near product storage. A batch is found to have rodent droppings.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.4 require?
options: A. Insects and rodents are a nuisance but not a GMP concern
B. Premises should be designed and equipped to afford maximum protection against entry of insects or other animals
C. Only rodent traps are sufficient
D. Pest control is optional for oral products
questions.explanation: Clause 3.4: 'Premises should be designed and equipped so as to afford maximum protection against the entry of insects or other animals.'

questions.scenario: Unauthorised personnel frequently walk through the production suite because no access control is in place. They use the area as a shortcut, and a visitor contaminates a batch.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.5 require?
options: A. No restrictions on movement
B. Steps should be taken to prevent entry of unauthorised people; production areas should not be used as a right of way
C. Only authorised personnel need to wear badges
D. A logbook is sufficient to control access
questions.explanation: Clause 3.5: 'Steps should be taken in order to prevent the entry of unauthorised people. Production, storage and quality control areas should not be used as a right of way by personnel who do not work in them.'

questions.scenario: A company manufactures penicillin and non‑penicillin products in the same area without dedicated HVAC. Trace penicillin is found in a non‑penicillin product, causing a patient allergic reaction.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.6 require in this situation?
options: A. Sharing equipment is acceptable with cleaning between batches
B. Cross‑contamination should be prevented; dedicated facilities are required for highly sensitising materials (e.g., beta‑lactams) when risk cannot be controlled
C. Only cleaning between campaigns is sufficient
D. No special measures are needed for penicillin
questions.explanation: Clause 3.6: 'Cross‑contamination should be prevented… Dedicated facilities are required for manufacturing when a medicinal product presents a risk because… allergenic potential from highly sensitising materials such as beta‑lactams.'

questions.scenario: The plant layout has weighing, mixing, and compression in a random arrangement. Materials must be moved back and forth across clean zones, causing cross‑contamination.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.7 recommend for layout?
options: A. Any layout is acceptable as long as cleaning is done
B. Premises should be laid out in a logical order corresponding to sequence of operations and cleanliness levels
C. All operations can be in one large room
D. Only the final packaging area needs segregation
questions.explanation: Clause 3.7: 'Premises should preferably be laid out in such a way as to allow the production to take place in areas connected in a logical order corresponding to the sequence of the operations and to the requisite cleanliness levels.'

questions.scenario: The production area is so cramped that different batches' materials are stored side by side without segregation. An operator mistakenly uses material from a different batch.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.8 require?
options: A. Space is not important if operators are careful
B. Adequate working and in‑process storage space to permit orderly positioning and minimise risk of confusion and cross‑contamination
C. Only the final product area needs space
D. Materials can be stored on the floor if labelled
questions.explanation: Clause 3.8: 'The adequacy of the working and in‑process storage space should permit the orderly and logical positioning of equipment and materials so as to minimise the risk of confusion between different medicinal products or their components, to avoid cross‑contamination…'

questions.scenario: The production room has cracked tiles on the floor and rough, unpainted walls that shed dust. The dust contaminates open product containers.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.9 require for interior surfaces where materials are exposed?
options: A. Any surface is acceptable if cleaned daily
B. Surfaces should be smooth, free from cracks and open joints, not shed particulate matter, and permit easy and effective cleaning
C. Only floors need to be smooth
D. Carpets are allowed if vacuumed
questions.explanation: Clause 3.9: 'Where starting and primary packaging materials, intermediate or bulk products are exposed to the environment, interior surfaces… should be smooth, free from cracks and open joints, and should not shed particulate matter and should permit easy and effective cleaning and, if necessary, disinfection.'

questions.scenario: Pipes and light fittings are installed with difficult‑to‑clean recesses. Maintenance requires entering production areas during operation, causing contamination.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.10 require?
options: A. Pipework design is not important
B. Pipework, light fittings, ventilation points should avoid recesses difficult to clean; for maintenance, they should be accessible from outside production areas
C. Maintenance can only be done during shutdown
D. No requirements for pipework
questions.explanation: Clause 3.10: 'Pipework, light fittings, ventilation points and other services should be designed and sited to avoid the creation of recesses which are difficult to clean. As far as possible, for maintenance purposes, they should be accessible from outside the manufacturing areas.'

questions.scenario: The production area has open drainage channels that are difficult to clean and become contaminated with standing water, leading to microbial growth.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.11 require for drains?
options: A. Open channels are acceptable if flushed regularly
B. Drains should be of adequate size, have trapped gullies; open channels avoided where possible; if necessary, shallow to facilitate cleaning and disinfection
C. Drains are not needed in production areas
D. Any drain design is acceptable
questions.explanation: Clause 3.11: 'Drains should be of adequate size, and have trapped gullies. Open channels should be avoided where possible, but if necessary, they should be shallow to facilitate cleaning and disinfection.'

questions.scenario: The production area has no HVAC; temperature and humidity fluctuate widely, and dust is not extracted. A humidity‑sensitive product degrades.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.12 require?
options: A. Natural ventilation is sufficient for oral products
B. Production areas should be effectively ventilated, with air control facilities (temperature, humidity, filtration) appropriate to products, operations, and external environment
C. Only temperature needs control
D. Ventilation is optional if the building is sealed
questions.explanation: Clause 3.12: 'Production areas should be effectively ventilated, with air control facilities (including temperature and, where necessary, humidity and filtration) appropriate both to the products handled, to the operations undertaken within them and to the external environment.'

questions.scenario: Weighing of active ingredients is done on an open bench in the main production corridor, next to other operations. Dust from nearby processes contaminates the weighed material.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.13 require?
options: A. Weighing can be done anywhere if the balance is covered
B. Weighing of starting materials usually should be carried out in a separate weighing room designed for such use
C. A portable screen is sufficient
D. Only the first weighing of the day needs a separate room
questions.explanation: Clause 3.13: 'Weighing of starting materials usually should be carried out in a separate weighing room designed for such use.'

questions.scenario: Dry powder mixing generates dust that spreads throughout the room; no local extraction is installed. Cross‑contamination occurs between products.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.14 require?
options: A. Dust is a normal part of manufacturing
B. In cases where dust is generated, specific provisions should be taken to avoid cross‑contamination and facilitate cleaning
C. Only wet processes need controls
D. Dust can be cleaned after the shift
questions.explanation: Clause 3.14: 'In cases where dust is generated (e.g. during sampling, weighing, mixing and processing operations, packaging of dry products), specific provisions should be taken to avoid cross‑contamination and facilitate cleaning.'

questions.scenario: Packaging lines for different products are next to each other without physical separation. Labels for different strengths are frequently mixed up, causing mislabelling.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.15 require?
options: A. No special design needed for packaging areas
B. Premises for packaging should be specifically designed and laid out to avoid mix‑ups or cross‑contamination
C. Only the printing area needs segregation
D. Colour coding is sufficient to prevent mix‑ups
questions.explanation: Clause 3.15: 'Premises for the packaging of medicinal products should be specifically designed and laid out so as to avoid mix‑ups or cross‑contamination.'

questions.scenario: The inspection area for filled vials is dimly lit; defects are missed, and a batch with cracked vials is released.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.16 require?
options: A. Lighting is not critical for visual inspection
B. Production areas should be well lit, particularly where visual on‑line controls are carried out
C. Only the ceiling lights matter
D. Natural light is sufficient
questions.explanation: Clause 3.16: 'Production areas should be well lit, particularly where visual on‑line controls are carried out.'

questions.scenario: In‑process pH testing is performed in the production area, but the testing spills acid onto exposed product, causing degradation.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.17 allow?
options: A. All testing must be done in the QC lab
B. In‑process controls may be carried out within the production area provided they do not carry any risk to production
C. No in‑process controls are allowed in production areas
D. Only visual checks can be done in production
questions.explanation: Clause 3.17: 'In‑process controls may be carried out within the production area provided they do not carry any risk to production.'

questions.scenario: The warehouse is so small that different categories of materials (quarantine, released, rejected) are stored together. A rejected batch is accidentally shipped.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.18 require?
options: A. One shelf is sufficient for all categories
B. Storage areas should have sufficient capacity to allow orderly storage of various categories (starting materials, intermediates, finished, quarantine, released, rejected, returned, recalled)
C. Only finished goods need separate storage
D. Rejected materials can be stored anywhere
questions.explanation: Clause 3.18: 'Storage areas should be of sufficient capacity to allow orderly storage of the various categories of materials and products: starting and packaging materials, intermediate, bulk and finished products, products in quarantine, released, rejected, returned or recalled.'

questions.scenario: A product requiring storage at 2–8°C is kept on an open shelf at room temperature for weeks. The product degrades and fails stability.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.19 require?
options: A. Room temperature is acceptable for all products if they are stable
B. Storage areas should be designed to ensure good storage conditions; clean, dry, within acceptable temperature limits; special conditions provided, checked, monitored
C. Only the label needs to state storage conditions
D. No monitoring of storage conditions is required
questions.explanation: Clause 3.19: 'Storage areas should be designed or adapted to ensure good storage conditions. In particular, they should be clean and dry and maintained within acceptable temperature limits. Where special storage conditions are required (e.g. temperature, humidity) these should be provided, checked and monitored.'

questions.scenario: The receiving bay has no roof; rain soaks incoming pallets of raw materials. Labels become illegible, and mould grows on cardboard containers.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.20 require?
options: A. Outdoor receipt is acceptable if materials are quickly moved inside
B. Receiving and dispatch bays should protect materials and products from the weather; reception areas should allow containers to be cleaned before storage
C. Only the inside of the warehouse matters
D. No special protection is needed for raw materials
questions.explanation: Clause 3.20: 'Receiving and dispatch bays should protect materials and products from the weather. Reception areas should be designed and equipped to allow containers of incoming materials to be cleaned where necessary before storage.'

questions.scenario: Quarantine is indicated only by a paper note that falls off. An operator uses the material before QC release, causing a contamination issue.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.21 require for quarantine?
options: A. A paper note is sufficient
B. Where quarantine is ensured by separate areas, those areas must be clearly marked and access restricted; any system replacing physical quarantine should give equivalent security
C. Only electronic tags are acceptable
D. Verbal notification of quarantine is enough
questions.explanation: Clause 3.21: 'Where quarantine status is ensured by storage in separate areas, these areas must be clearly marked and their access restricted to authorised personnel. Any system replacing the physical quarantine should give equivalent security.'

questions.scenario: Raw material samples are taken in the main storage area without precautions. A sample dipper is reused for different materials, causing cross‑contamination.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.22 require?
options: A. Sampling can be done anywhere if the operator is careful
B. There should normally be a separate sampling area for starting materials; if sampling in storage area, it must prevent contamination/cross‑contamination
C. No sampling is needed for raw materials
D. Only QC personnel can sample, regardless of location
questions.explanation: Clause 3.22: 'There should normally be a separate sampling area for starting materials. If sampling is performed in the storage area, it should be conducted in such a way as to prevent contamination or cross‑contamination.'

questions.scenario: Rejected batches are stored on the same shelves as released products. A rejected batch is accidentally shipped to a customer.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.23 require?
options: A. No segregation is needed if rejected materials are labelled
B. Segregated areas should be provided for storage of rejected, recalled or returned materials or products
C. A red sticker is sufficient to identify rejected materials
D. Rejected materials can be stored with released products if they are in sealed containers
questions.explanation: Clause 3.23: 'Segregated areas should be provided for the storage of rejected, recalled or returned materials or products.'

questions.scenario: Highly potent hormones are stored in an unlocked cabinet in a general warehouse with unrestricted access. Unauthorised personnel remove material, leading to a theft incident.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.24 require?
options: A. No special storage is needed for potent materials
B. Highly active materials or products should be stored in safe and secure areas
C. A simple lock is optional
D. They can be stored with other products if labelled
questions.explanation: Clause 3.24: 'Highly active materials or products should be stored in safe and secure areas.'

questions.scenario: Printed labels are left on an open shelf. An unauthorised person takes labels and uses them to mislabel counterfeit product.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.25 require?
options: A. No special security for labels
B. Printed packaging materials are critical; special attention should be paid to safe and secure storage
C. A logbook for label use is sufficient
D. Labels can be stored with other packaging materials
questions.explanation: Clause 3.25: 'Printed packaging materials are considered critical to the conformity of the medicinal product and special attention should be paid to the safe and secure storage of these materials.'

questions.scenario: The QC lab is inside the production area. Dust from production enters the lab and contaminates samples, causing false test results.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.26 require?
options: A. No separation is needed if the lab is cleaned frequently
B. Normally, QC laboratories should be separated from production areas, especially for biologicals, microbiologicals, radioisotopes
C. A door is sufficient separation
D. Only microbiology labs need separation
questions.explanation: Clause 3.26: 'Normally, Quality Control laboratories should be separated from production areas. This is particularly important for laboratories for the control of biologicals, microbiologicals and radioisotopes, which should also be separated from each other.'

questions.scenario: The control lab is so cramped that samples are stored on the floor, and different testing activities overlap. A sample is misidentified, leading to a wrong batch rejection.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.27 require?
options: A. Any space is fine as long as testing is done
B. Control laboratories should be designed to suit operations; sufficient space to avoid mix‑ups and cross‑contamination; adequate storage for samples and records
C. Only the instrument room needs space
D. No storage is needed for samples
questions.explanation: Clause 3.27: 'Control laboratories should be designed to suit the operations to be carried out in them. Sufficient space should be given to avoid mix‑ups and cross‑contamination. There should be adequate suitable storage space for samples and records.'

questions.scenario: A precision balance used for assay is placed next to a vibrating blender. The vibration causes erratic readings, and a batch is wrongly approved.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.28 allow?
options: A. No separation is needed for instruments
B. Separate rooms may be necessary to protect sensitive instruments from vibration, electrical interference, humidity, etc.
C. Instruments can be anywhere as long as they are calibrated
D. Only humidity control is important
questions.explanation: Clause 3.28: 'Separate rooms may be necessary to protect sensitive instruments from vibration, electrical interference, humidity, etc.'

questions.scenario: A laboratory handling radioactive samples has no special containment or waste disposal procedures. A spill contaminates the area.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.29 state?
options: A. No special requirements for radioactive samples
B. Special requirements are needed in laboratories handling particular substances, such as biological or radioactive samples
C. General laboratory rules apply
D. Only biological samples need special handling
questions.explanation: Clause 3.29: 'Special requirements are needed in laboratories handling particular substances, such as biological or radioactive samples.'

questions.scenario: Employees eat lunch at their workbenches in the production area. Food crumbs fall into open product containers, causing contamination.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.30 require?
options: A. Eating is allowed if the area is cleaned afterwards
B. Rest and refreshment rooms should be separate from other areas
C. A designated corner in the production area is acceptable
D. No separate rooms are needed if employees wash hands
questions.explanation: Clause 3.30: 'Rest and refreshment rooms should be separate from other areas.'

questions.scenario: Toilets open directly into the production corridor; there are no facilities for changing clothes. Operators wear street clothes in production.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.31 require?
options: A. Toilets can open into production if they are cleaned often
B. Facilities for changing clothes and washing/toilet should be easily accessible; toilets should not directly communicate with production or storage areas
C. Only hand sanitiser is needed at the production entrance
D. Toilets inside production areas are acceptable if door is kept closed
questions.explanation: Clause 3.31: 'Facilities for changing clothes and for washing and toilet purposes should be easily accessible and appropriate for the number of users. Toilets should not directly communicate with production or storage areas.'

questions.scenario: Maintenance tools and parts are stored on open racks in the production area. Dust and grease from tools contaminate product containers.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.32 require?
options: A. Tools can be stored anywhere if cleaned before use
B. Maintenance workshops should be separated from production areas; parts/tools stored in production should be in reserved rooms or lockers
C. Only large tools need segregation
D. No separation is needed if tools are covered
questions.explanation: Clause 3.32: 'Maintenance workshops should as far as possible be separated from production areas. Whenever parts and tools are stored in the production area, they should be kept in rooms or lockers reserved for that use.'

questions.scenario: An animal house for quality control testing is located next to the production area, with shared ventilation. Allergens from animals contaminate the production suite.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.33 require?
options: A. Animal houses can be adjacent if air pressure is balanced
B. Animal houses should be well isolated from other areas, with separate entrance and air handling
C. Only a door is needed for separation
D. Animals can be kept in production if they are caged
questions.explanation: Clause 3.33: 'Animal houses should be well isolated from other areas, with separate entrance (animal access) and air handling facilities.'

questions.scenario: A reactor is installed in a corner where it cannot be properly cleaned, and no maintenance plan exists. Residue builds up and contaminates subsequent batches.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.34 require?
options: A. Equipment can be installed anywhere as long as it works
B. Manufacturing equipment should be designed, located and maintained to suit its intended purpose
C. Only new equipment needs to be properly located
D. Maintenance is optional for equipment
questions.explanation: Clause 3.34: 'Manufacturing equipment should be designed, located and maintained to suit its intended purpose.'

questions.scenario: During maintenance, an operator leaves a metal shaving inside a mixing vessel. The shaving later contaminates a batch and damages downstream equipment.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.35 require?
options: A. Maintenance does not need special precautions
B. Repair and maintenance operations should not present any hazard to the quality of the products
C. Only cleaning after maintenance is needed
D. Hazards are acceptable if documented
questions.explanation: Clause 3.35: 'Repair and maintenance operations should not present any hazard to the quality of the products.'

questions.scenario: Equipment is cleaned irregularly; after cleaning, it is stored wet, leading to microbial growth. The next batch is contaminated.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.36 require?
options: A. Cleaning can be any method
B. Manufacturing equipment should be designed for easy and thorough cleaning; cleaned according to written procedures; stored only in clean and dry condition
C. Storage condition is not important
D. No written procedures are needed for cleaning
questions.explanation: Clause 3.36: 'Manufacturing equipment should be designed so that it can be easily and thoroughly cleaned. It should be cleaned according to detailed and written procedures and stored only in a clean and dry condition.'

questions.scenario: The same mop and bucket are used to clean all equipment, without disinfection. Cross‑contamination occurs between different product contact surfaces.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.37 require?
options: A. Any cleaning equipment is acceptable
B. Washing and cleaning equipment should be chosen and used in order not to be a source of contamination
C. Only the cleaning solution matters
D. Disinfection is optional
questions.explanation: Clause 3.37: 'Washing and cleaning equipment should be chosen and used in order not to be a source of contamination.'

questions.scenario: Equipment is installed without proper alignment; product leaks through a poorly fitted gasket, causing contamination.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.38 require?
options: A. Installation is not critical for product quality
B. Equipment should be installed in such a way as to prevent any risk of error or of contamination
C. Only electrical connections need to be correct
D. Leaks are acceptable if they are collected
questions.explanation: Clause 3.38: 'Equipment should be installed in such a way as to prevent any risk of error or of contamination.'

questions.scenario: A plastic container used for an organic solvent leaches plasticisers into the product. The product fails toxicity testing.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.39 require?
options: A. Any material is acceptable if it is cheap
B. Parts of production equipment that contact product must not be reactive, additive or absorptive to such an extent that it affects quality
C. Only metal equipment is allowed
D. Leaching is acceptable below a certain limit without testing
questions.explanation: Clause 3.39: 'Parts of production equipment that come into contact with the product must not be reactive, additive or absorptive to such an extent that it will affect the quality of the product and thus present any hazard.'

questions.scenario: A balance with 1 g readability is used to weigh a 5 mg active ingredient, leading to large dosing errors. The batch fails potency testing.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.40 require?
options: A. Any balance can be used if it is calibrated
B. Balances and measuring equipment of an appropriate range and precision should be available for production and control operations
C. Only the QC lab needs precision balances
D. Approximate weighing is acceptable for non‑critical ingredients
questions.explanation: Clause 3.40: 'Balances and measuring equipment of an appropriate range and precision should be available for production and control operations.'

questions.scenario: A pH meter used for a critical reaction has not been calibrated for two years. The reaction fails because the pH was incorrect.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.41 require?
options: A. Calibration is only needed when results look wrong
B. Measuring, weighing, recording and control equipment should be calibrated and checked at defined intervals; records maintained
C. One calibration at installation is sufficient
D. No calibration records are required
questions.explanation: Clause 3.41: 'Measuring, weighing, recording and control equipment should be calibrated and checked at defined intervals by appropriate methods. Adequate records of such tests should be maintained.'

questions.scenario: In a plant, pipes are not labelled. An operator connects the wrong solvent to a reactor, causing a violent reaction and batch failure.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.42 require?
options: A. Labelling is optional if operators are experienced
B. Fixed pipework should be clearly labelled to indicate the contents and, where applicable, the direction of flow
C. Only hazardous pipes need labels
D. Colour coding without text is sufficient
questions.explanation: Clause 3.42: 'Fixed pipework should be clearly labelled to indicate the contents and, where applicable, the direction of flow.'

questions.scenario: The purified water loop is never sanitised; microbial counts exceed action limits, and product is contaminated with biofilm.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.43 require?
options: A. No sanitisation is needed if water tests pass
B. Distilled, deionised and other water pipes should be sanitised according to written procedures that detail action limits for microbiological contamination and measures to be taken
C. Sanitisation once a year is enough
D. Only if product is injectable
questions.explanation: Clause 3.43: 'Distilled, deionised and, where appropriate, other water pipes should be sanitised according to written procedures that detail the action limits for microbiological contamination and the measures to be taken.'

questions.scenario: A faulty tablet press is left in the production area without any label. An operator uses it and produces defective tablets.
questions.question: What does Clause 3.44 require?
options: A. Defective equipment can stay as long as it is not used
B. Defective equipment should, if possible, be removed; at least clearly labelled as defective
C. Only remove if it is expensive
D. No action is needed until it is repaired
questions.explanation: Clause 3.44: 'Defective equipment should, if possible, be removed from production and quality control areas, or at least be clearly labelled as defective.'

questions.scenario: A company uses a mix of paper and electronic records but has no defined controls for master documents or data integrity. Old electronic files are not validated, and data is lost.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.1 require?
options: A. Only paper documents need control
B. All document types must be defined; controls for electronic documents, templates, master documents; integrity of record throughout retention
C. Electronic documents do not need validation
D. No special controls are needed for hybrid systems
questions.explanation: Clause 4.1: 'All types of document should be defined and adhered to… Appropriate controls for electronic documents such as templates, forms, and master documents should be implemented. Appropriate controls should be in place to ensure the integrity of the record throughout the retention period.'

questions.scenario: Working copies of master documents are photocopied poorly, causing missing text. No review of copies is performed. An operator follows an incomplete instruction and makes an error.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.2 require regarding reproduction of documents?
options: A. Any reproduction method is acceptable
B. Reproduction of working documents from master documents should not allow any error to be introduced through the reproduction process
C. Only electronic copies are allowed
D. Master documents are not needed for routine operations
questions.explanation: Clause 4.2: 'The reproduction of working documents from master documents should not allow any error to be introduced through the reproduction process.'

questions.scenario: A new SOP is issued without approval signatures or an effective date. The document has no unique identifier. Operators use an outdated version by mistake.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.3 require for documents containing instructions?
options: A. No approval is needed for internal documents
B. Documents should be approved, signed and dated by appropriate persons; have unambiguous contents, be uniquely identifiable; effective date defined
C. Only the effective date matters
D. Verbal approval from the manager is sufficient
questions.explanation: Clause 4.3: 'Documents containing instructions should be approved, signed and dated by appropriate and authorised persons. Documents should have unambiguous contents and be uniquely identifiable. The effective date should be defined.'

questions.scenario: A manufacturing instruction is written in a long, confusing paragraph style. Operators frequently misinterpret the steps, leading to deviations.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.4 say about document style?
options: A. Any style is acceptable as long as the information is there
B. Documents should be laid out in an orderly fashion, easy to check; SOPs should be written in an imperative mandatory style
C. Only bullet points are allowed
D. Style is irrelevant if operators are trained
questions.explanation: Clause 4.4: 'Documents containing instructions should be laid out in an orderly fashion and be easy to check… Standard Operating Procedures, Work Instructions and Methods should be written in an imperative mandatory style.'

questions.scenario: A new version of a cleaning SOP is issued, but the old version remains on the production floor. An operator uses the old SOP and misses a critical cleaning step, causing cross‑contamination.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.5 require regarding superseded documents?
options: A. Old versions can be kept alongside new ones for reference
B. Systems should be operated to prevent inadvertent use of superseded documents
C. Only the new version needs to be stored
D. No control is needed if the old version is marked 'obsolete' but still present
questions.explanation: Clause 4.5: 'When a document has been revised, systems should be operated to prevent inadvertent use of superseded documents.'

questions.scenario: A batch record has no space for entering actual yields. The operator writes numbers in the margin, and some numbers are illegible.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.6 require regarding document design?
options: A. Space is not required; operators can use margins
B. Documents should not be hand‑written; where data entry is required, sufficient space should be provided
C. Handwritten entries are always forbidden
D. Space is optional if the operator has good handwriting
questions.explanation: Clause 4.6: 'Documents should not be hand‑written; although, where documents require the entry of data, sufficient space should be provided for such entries.'

questions.scenario: An analyst records a test result in pencil. Later, the number is erased and changed without trace. The batch is released based on the altered result.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.7 require for handwritten entries?
options: A. Pencil is acceptable if it is dark
B. Handwritten entries should be made in clear, legible, indelible way
C. Only ballpoint pen is allowed, but erasures are still possible
D. Indelible means any ink, even if erasable
questions.explanation: Clause 4.7: 'Handwritten entries should be made in clear, legible, indelible way.'

questions.scenario: At the end of a shift, an operator completes the batch record from memory. Several times and yields are recorded incorrectly, leading to a batch failure.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.8 require regarding the timing of records?
options: A. Records can be completed at the end of the batch if the operator has a good memory
B. Records should be made or completed at the time each action is taken
C. Only electronic records need to be real‑time
D. The supervisor can back‑date entries if necessary
questions.explanation: Clause 4.8: 'Records should be made or completed at the time each action is taken and in such a way that all significant activities concerning the manufacture of medicinal products are traceable.'

questions.scenario: A QC analyst makes a mistake in a laboratory notebook. He scribbles out the original value, writes a new one, and does not sign or date the change. An investigator cannot determine who made the change.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.9 require for alterations?
options: A. Any alteration is acceptable if the new value is correct
B. Any alteration should be signed and dated; the original information must remain legible; the reason should be recorded where appropriate
C. Only the date is required for the alteration
D. No signature is needed if the alteration is minor
questions.explanation: Clause 4.9: 'Any alteration made to the entry on a document should be signed and dated; the alteration should permit the reading of the original information. Where appropriate, the reason for the alteration should be recorded.'

questions.scenario: A company cannot locate the raw data for a stability study because records are stored in an uncontrolled manner. The study is invalidated.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.10 require regarding record location and integrity?
options: A. Records can be stored anywhere as long as they are not lost
B. It should be clearly defined which record is related to each manufacturing activity and where it is located; secure controls to ensure integrity throughout retention
C. No need to define location if records are electronic
D. Only electronic records need controls
questions.explanation: Clause 4.10: 'It should be clearly defined which record is related to each manufacturing activity and where this record is located. Secure controls must be in place to ensure the integrity of the record throughout the retention period and validated where appropriate.'

questions.scenario: A batch documentation is kept for only two years after batch expiry, but national law requires five years after certification. An inspection finds a violation.
questions.question: What retention period does Clause 4.11 specify for batch documentation?
options: A. 1 year after expiry or at least 5 years after certification, whichever is longer
B. 10 years regardless
C. Only 2 years after expiry
D. No specific period is given
questions.explanation: Clause 4.11: 'Batch documentation must be kept for one year after expiry of the batch to which it relates or at least five years after certification of the batch by the Authorised Person, whichever is the longer.'

questions.scenario: The company discards raw data from a process validation study after 6 months, even though the marketing authorisation is still valid. A regulator requests the data and it is missing.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.12 say about retention of critical documentation supporting a marketing authorisation?
options: A. It can be discarded after 1 year
B. Critical documentation, including raw data, supporting the MA should be retained whilst the authorisation remains in force
C. Only the final report needs retention
D. No retention is needed for validation data
questions.explanation: Clause 4.12: 'Critical documentation, including raw data (for example relating to validation or stability), which supports information in the Marketing Authorisation should be retained whilst the authorisation remains in force.'

questions.scenario: A manufacturer uses starting materials without authorised specifications. No approval date is on the specification document, and the wrong material is used.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.13 require?
options: A. Specifications are optional for starting materials
B. There should be appropriately authorised and dated specifications for starting and packaging materials, and finished products
C. Only finished products need specifications
D. No authorisation is needed for internal specifications
questions.explanation: Clause 4.13: 'There should be appropriately authorised and dated specifications for starting and packaging materials, and finished products.'

questions.scenario: A specification for printed labels lacks a specimen and does not list approved suppliers. A label from an unapproved supplier is used, causing misprinting.
questions.question: What must specifications for packaging materials include per Clause 4.14?
options: A. Only the material name

B. Description including designated name, internal code, pharmacopoeial reference, approved suppliers, specimen of printed materials, sampling directions, requirements, storage conditions, retest period
C. Only the supplier name
D. Only the storage conditions
questions.explanation: Clause 4.14 lists the required elements: description (name, code, monograph, suppliers, specimen), sampling and testing directions, qualitative/quantitative requirements, storage conditions, maximum storage period before re‑examination.

questions.scenario: A company purchases an intermediate but has no specification for it. The material is used without testing and causes a batch failure.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.15 require for intermediate and bulk products?
options: A. No specification is needed for intermediates
B. Specifications should be available for critical steps or if purchased/dispatched; similar to starting materials or finished products specifications
C. Only finished products need specifications
D. Intermediate specs are optional if they are not sold
questions.explanation: Clause 4.15: 'Specifications for intermediate and bulk products should be available for critical steps or if these are purchased or dispatched. The specifications should be similar to specifications for starting materials or for finished products, as appropriate.'

questions.scenario: A finished product specification does not include the formula or storage conditions. The batch is released with incorrect storage instructions, leading to product degradation.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.16 require a finished product specification to include?
options: A. Only the product name
B. Designated name, formula, description of pharmaceutical form and package details, sampling/testing directions, qualitative/quantitative requirements, storage conditions, shelf‑life
C. Only the shelf‑life
D. Only the storage conditions
questions.explanation: Clause 4.16 lists the required elements for finished product specifications: designated name, formula, description, directions for sampling and testing, qualitative/quantitative requirements, storage conditions, shelf‑life.

questions.scenario: A manufacturing formula does not include the expected yield limits. The operator has no target to compare actual yield, and a significant loss goes unnoticed.
questions.question: What must the manufacturing formula include per Clause 4.17?
options: A. Only the list of materials
B. Product name, description, batch size, list of starting materials with amounts, statement of expected final yield with acceptable limits and relevant intermediate yields
C. Only the batch size
D. Only the product name
questions.explanation: Clause 4.17 requires: product name, description, batch size, list of starting materials with amounts, statement of expected final yield with acceptable limits, and relevant intermediate yields where applicable.

questions.scenario: The processing instructions do not include checks that the equipment is clean before use. A batch is contaminated with residue from a previous product.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.18 require processing instructions to include?
options: A. Only the stepwise processing

B. Processing location, principal equipment, methods for preparing critical equipment (cleaning, assembling, sterilising), checks that equipment and work station are clear of previous products, stepwise instructions, in-process controls, bulk storage requirements, special precautions
C. Only the stepwise instructions
D. Only the in-process controls
questions.explanation: Clause 4.18 lists the required elements: processing location, principal equipment, methods for preparing critical equipment (e.g. cleaning, assembling, sterilising), checks for cleanliness and suitability, detailed stepwise instructions, in-process controls with limits, bulk storage requirements, special precautions.

questions.scenario: Packaging instructions for a product do not specify the checks for line clearance before packaging. A leftover label from a previous product is used, causing mislabelling.
questions.question: What must packaging instructions include per Clause 4.19?
options: A. Only the list of packaging materials

B. Name of product, description, pack size, complete list of packaging materials with codes, example of printed materials, checks for line clearance, special precautions, description of operation, in-process controls
C. Only the line clearance checks
D. Only the packaging materials list
questions.explanation: Clause 4.19 details the required content: product name, description, pack size, complete list of packaging materials, example of printed materials, line clearance checks, special precautions, description of packaging operation, in-process controls.

questions.scenario: A batch processing record does not include the product yield at intermediate stages. A discrepancy goes undetected, and a batch with low yield is released.
questions.question: What information must a batch processing record contain per Clause 4.20?
options: A. Only the final yield

B. Name and batch number, dates and times, operator identification, batch numbers and quantities of starting materials, processing events, in-process control results, product yields at pertinent stages, notes on deviations, approval signature
C. Only the in-process controls
D. Only the operator names
questions.explanation: Clause 4.20 lists: product name and batch number, dates and times, operator identifications, batch numbers and quantities of starting materials, processing events, in-process control results, product yields at different stages, notes on deviations, approval by responsible person.

questions.scenario: A batch packaging record does not include samples of printed packaging materials used, and reconciliation shows a discrepancy that is not explained. The missing labels are later found on mislabelled bottles.
questions.question: What must a batch packaging record include per Clause 4.21?
options: A. Only the quantities

B. Product name and batch number, dates and times, operator identification, checks for identity and conformity, details of operations, samples of printed materials, notes on deviations, reconciliation of quantities, approval
C. Only the reconciliation
D. Only the samples of printed materials
questions.explanation: Clause 4.21 requires: product name and batch number, dates and times, operator identification, records of checks, details of packaging operations, samples of printed materials, notes on deviations, reconciliation of quantities, approval.

questions.scenario: A manufacturer has no written procedure for receipt of starting materials. A delivery with damaged containers is accepted without investigation, and the material is used.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.22 require?
options: A. Verbal instructions are enough for receipt
B. There should be written procedures and records for the receipt of each delivery of each starting material, primary, secondary and printed packaging materials
C. No procedure is needed if the supplier is approved
D. Only for active substances
questions.explanation: Clause 4.22: 'There should be written procedures and records for the receipt of each delivery of each starting material, (including bulk, intermediate or finished goods), primary, secondary and printed packaging materials.'

questions.scenario: A receipt record for a raw material does not include the supplier's name or the batch number assigned after receipt. During a recall, the supplier cannot be traced.
questions.question: What information must be included in receipt records per Clause 4.23?
options: A. Only the date

B. Name of material, in‑house code, date of receipt, supplier's name and manufacturer's name, manufacturer's batch number, total quantity and number of containers, batch number assigned, relevant comments
C. Only the quantity
D. Only the supplier's name
questions.explanation: Clause 4.23 lists the required elements: name on delivery note and containers, in‑house name/code, date of receipt, supplier's name and manufacturer's name, manufacturer's batch/reference number, total quantity and number of containers, batch number assigned after receipt, any relevant comment.

questions.scenario: There is no written procedure for internal labelling, quarantine, and storage of starting materials. A material in quarantine is mistakenly used in production.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.24 require?
options: A. No procedure is needed; operators can decide
B. There should be written procedures for internal labelling, quarantine and storage of starting materials, packaging materials and other materials, as appropriate
C. Only labelling is needed
D. Only quarantine is needed
questions.explanation: Clause 4.24: 'There should be written procedures for the internal labeling, quarantine and storage of starting materials, packaging materials and other materials, as appropriate.'

questions.scenario: Sampling is performed without a written procedure. A sample is taken with a dirty dipper, contaminating the bulk material and causing a batch failure.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.25 require for sampling?
options: A. No procedure is needed if the sampler is experienced
B. There should be written procedures for sampling, including methods, equipment, amounts, and precautions to avoid contamination or deterioration
C. Only the amount to be taken needs to be documented
D. Only the method needs to be described
questions.explanation: Clause 4.25: 'There should be written procedures for sampling, which include the methods and equipment to be used, the amounts to be taken and any precautions to be observed to avoid contamination of the material or any deterioration in its quality.'

questions.scenario: A QC laboratory uses a non‑validated test method and does not record the test results. The batch is released without proper documentation, and a later failure is traced to the missing records.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.26 require?
options: A. No procedure is needed for testing
B. There should be written procedures for testing materials and products at different stages; the tests performed should be recorded
C. Only the results need to be recorded, not the procedure
D. Procedures are optional if the method is standard
questions.explanation: Clause 4.26: 'There should be written procedures for testing materials and products at different stages of manufacture, describing the methods and equipment to be used. The tests performed should be recorded.'

questions.scenario: The company has no written release or rejection procedure. An Authorised Person releases a batch without reviewing all records, and a contaminated batch is released.
questions.question: What does Clause 4.27 require?
options: A. No procedure is needed; the Authorised Person can decide case‑by‑case

B. Written release and rejection procedures should be available, especially for certification by the Authorised Person; all records available to the Authorised Person; system to indicate special observations and changes to critical data
C. Only a verbal approval is enough
D. Only a signature on the certificate is required
questions.explanation: Clause 4.27: 'Written release and rejection procedures should be available for materials and products, and in particular for the certification for sale of the finished product by the Authorised Person(s).
